nodes.label: ADR 0006: any member may reap an orphaned inbox, on age plus absence
nodes.rationale: Status accepted, implemented in 0.10.0. Nothing ever deletes a message from a peer's inbox except that peer, so mail addressed to a peer that never comes back is unreachable garbage. Measured: after compacting a trial repository from 3,075 commits and 433 MB to a single commit, 60 MB survived for a live tree of 17 files, almost entirely two abandoned 30 MiB payloads in dead ephemeral peers' inboxes plus stale beacons.

nodes.label: Workspace.reap()
nodes.rationale: The reaper lives in Workspace beside queues(), reusing its listing and key parsing, so core stays pure mechanism and gains no dependency on the runtime. Eight guards, each confirmed by removing it and watching a named test fail.

nodes.label: Stale presence beacon reaper (aggressive)
nodes.rationale: Any peer deletes a beacon at ws/<workspace>/peers/<peer>.ddf whose announcedAt is older than a small multiple of presenceTtlMs. A beacon is self-healing: a live peer rewrites it every presenceIntervalMs (30s default), so deleting one wrongly costs at most one interval of invisibility to discover.

nodes.label: Orphaned inbox object reaper (conservative)
nodes.rationale: Deletes ws/<workspace>/inbox/<peer>/<id>.ddf only when all three hold: the peer is not this peer, the object is older than inboxOrphanMs, and the owning peer has no beacon at all or a beacon older than inboxOrphanMs. A message is not self-healing and deleting one wrongly is unrecoverable, so it gets a far longer horizon than a beacon; collapsing the two would either leak beacons for a week or destroy mail in minutes.

nodes.label: inboxOrphanMs horizon
nodes.rationale: Default 7 days, 0 disables and restores today's behaviour exactly. A backstop against abandonment, not an expiry mechanism; a message with no TTL at all is still subject to it. The 7 day default sits far beyond a closed laptop and far below forever. Clock skew between peers shifts the effective horizon by the skew, which at 7 days needs extraordinary skew to matter.

nodes.label: Age comes from the key, never the payload
nodes.rationale: parseInboxKey returns the message id and idTime decodes a creation timestamp from it. Cost: deciding by download would mean fetching every object in every inbox on every cycle, reading the entire leak in order to decide to delete it. Availability: modifiedAt is optional in the store contract and backend-dependent, while the id is the sender's own clock and always present. Same reasoning reapTopics already applies, from the 'age unknown is not old enough to delete' lesson.

nodes.label: idTime / parseInboxKey
nodes.rationale: parseInboxKey returns the message id; idTime decodes a creation timestamp out of it. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is decrypted to make a reaping decision.

nodes.label: reapTopics (mailbox.ts:700)
nodes.rationale: Covers broadcast topics only, and already takes age from the id at mailbox.ts:716 for the same availability reasons.

nodes.label: core/mailbox.ts delivery loop
nodes.rationale: mailbox.ts:434 polls inboxPrefix(workspace, this.peerId), the peer's own inbox and nothing else. TTL expiry at mailbox.ts:548 fires inside that peer's own loop, so it never runs for a peer that is gone.

nodes.label: queues() diagnostic (runtime/workspace.ts:575)
nodes.rationale: The only caller that lists inboxRoot, the all-peers prefix, and it deletes nothing. reap() reuses its listing and key parsing.

nodes.label: isExpired / per-message TTL
nodes.rationale: isExpired reads ttlMs and ts from the envelope header, and that header is encrypted. Honouring a message's real TTL from outside its recipient would require decrypting every candidate, so orphan reaping is explicitly not TTL and must not be described as one.

nodes.label: Absence of a beacon as the liveness signal
nodes.rationale: stop() calls withdraw() (workspace.ts:290 and :844), which deletes the peer's own beacon, so a cleanly exited peer leaves no beacon and a populated inbox, which is exactly the measured case. A crashed peer leaves a beacon that stops being refreshed. 'No beacon, or one older than the horizon' covers both. Age alone would be wrong: a peer offline over a holiday has old messages and is not orphaned. Requiring both conditions separates 'gone' from 'not looking right now'.

nodes.label: discoverPeers({ includeStale: true }) / listBeacons
nodes.rationale: Already returns announce times for every beacon it can read. It skips beacons it cannot decode, which is why listBeacons returns the objects it found separately from the records it decoded.

nodes.label: A partial view is not a view
nodes.rationale: Absence of a beacon is the entire liveness signal, so a store that failed to answer is indistinguishable from a workspace where nobody is alive. The pass deletes nothing unless every store answered; without that, one transient outage on a multi-transport workspace clears every inbox.

nodes.label: An undecodable beacon still counts as liveness
nodes.rationale: Beacons that cannot be read belong to a key era this peer does not hold, and their owners may be perfectly alive, so the existence of the object is the signal and its contents are not required.

nodes.label: A stale beacon is kept while its owner still has mail
nodes.rationale: A beacon goes stale in fifteen minutes and mail lives seven days, so the beacon reaper would routinely destroy the one piece of evidence telling the next pass that a backlog belongs to someone recently alive. The beacon follows on a later pass once the mail is reaped.

nodes.label: Shared reaper throttle on the presence interval
nodes.rationale: The 'same poll cycle as reapTopics' idea was a MailboxEngine notion and the engine's poll is not visible from Workspace, so the pass rides the presence interval and carries its own throttle of ten presenceTtlMs, fifteen minutes at defaults. Cheap because on git and github a listing reads the working tree the mailbox poll already keeps fresh. The pass does not run during start(), since start-up had already moved the first beacon off its critical path and a full inbox listing is much heavier than one put.

nodes.label: Ephemeral <configured>-c<pid-hex> connect peers
nodes.rationale: Every ddrop connect runs its own runtime under an ephemeral identity, so each invocation can strand whatever was in flight when it exited. Measured culprits: peer-b-c2192 and peer-b-c14c9e.

nodes.label: Reaping grants no new privilege
nodes.rationale: Every member already holds the workspace secret and can fetch and decode any object in any inbox, and every member already has unrestricted delete because authorisation lives in the transport's access control, not in dead-drop. A hostile member can wipe every inbox today with no code from this ADR. What changes is that correct peers now delete data they did not author, so the risk to design against is accidental loss, not privilege escalation.

nodes.label: allowPeers guardrail
nodes.rationale: Documented in docs/security-model.md as a guardrail rather than a boundary, and it cannot be used with ddrop connect at all.

nodes.label: Invariant 9 (keys carry names in the clear by design)
nodes.rationale: Untouched by reaping: the reaper reads object keys, which already carry workspace and peer names by documented design, and decrypts nothing.

nodes.label: Rejected: reaping by peer-id shape
nodes.rationale: Matching the <configured>-c<pid-hex> pattern identifies the measured culprit precisely and is still the wrong mechanism: it hard-codes a naming convention into a destructive operation and misses every orphan that did not come from connect.

nodes.label: Rejected: an owner or elected reaper
nodes.rationale: No election exists, ADR 0005 already set the precedent that any peer may perform maintenance when the operation itself is safe, and a single designated reaper is a single point of failure for a leak that only matters over months.

nodes.label: Rejected: honouring real per-message TTL by decrypting candidates
nodes.rationale: Correct, and it costs a full download of everything under consideration on every cycle.

nodes.label: Rejected: sender-side expiry
nodes.rationale: By the time a message is orphaned the sender is usually gone too, since the common case is an ephemeral connect peer on both ends.

nodes.label: Rejected: doing nothing because compaction bounds the repository
nodes.rationale: Measured false: 60 MB survived compaction and survives every future compaction, because preserving the live tree is what compaction is for.

nodes.label: A failed or refused delete is not retried every cycle
nodes.rationale: The trap ADR 0005 hit: a maintenance condition that stays true after a failure turns into a wasted network call on every poll, forever. Reaping also logs at warn, naming the peer, object count and bytes, because a destructive unattended action has to be visible in ddrop logs.
